stories.headline: INDIA bloc leaders pass motion seeking impeachment of Chief Election Commissioner
stories.title: INDIA bloc leaders pass motion seeking impeachment of Chief Election Commissioner
stories.summary: New Delhi, Oct 31: The Congress-led INDIA bloc on Saturday held a mock ‘public impeachment’ of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar at Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge’s residence, accusing him of electoral malpractice and demanding his removal. Kharge moved a resolution seeking Gyanesh Kumar’s removal, alleging that he had acted against the interests of democracy. Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi, other Opposition MPs, jurists, lawyers and civil society members attended the meeting, which was presided over by former Lok Sabha Speaker Meira Kumar. Kharge listed six charges against the CEC, including conspiring to steal elections, deleting 13.2 crore voters from electoral rolls, rewriting Form 6 applications, and taking control of electoral rolls through ECINET. The Opposition also accused Gyanesh Kumar of ignoring the views of the other two Election Commissioners and working at the behest of Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Home Minister Amit Shah. Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi said Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar would not continue in office, claiming that the Opposition had enough evidence to ensure his removal. ANI meanwhile reports that INDIA bloc leaders passed a motion seeking the impeachment of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar during a symbolic public impeachment programme organised against him. The event was held to register the opposition bloc’s protest against the CEC. Congress MP Shashi Tharoor, according to PTI described the INDIA bloc’s ‘Mock Parliament’, held at party president Mallikarjun Kharge’s residence in Delhi, as a dignified and constructive discussion reflecting a strong commitment to protecting Indian democracy. Following the meeting, Tharoor said the same spirit would carry forward to the bloc’s Maha Rally at Ramlila Maidan, where lakhs of people are expected to participate tomorrow. The meeting was organised after authorities denied permission for holding it at Ramlila Maidan. The INDIA bloc raised three key demands: restoration of names of voters allegedly removed from electoral rolls, removal of the CEC and repeal of the law granting immunity to the Chief Election Commissioner. The Opposition is also scheduled to hold a rally at Ramlila Maidan on November 1 as part of its ‘vote chori’ campaign against the Election Commission and the Centre.

stories.headline: India's opposition set to hold mega rally seeking election chief's resignation
stories.title: India's opposition set to hold mega rally seeking election chief's resignation
stories.summary: It comes amid growing protests over a voter roll revision exercise feared to leave 130 million voters off rolls.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Tens of thousands of people are expected to gather in the Indian capital, Delhi, for a mega opposition rally, seeking the resignation of chief election commissioner and electoral reforms.
The rally, called by the main opposition Congress party, will begin around noon at the famous Ramlila Maidan grounds, with leaders claiming a million people could attend.
Several top leaders of the Congress-led INDIA alliance have said they would attend and the influential Gen Z-led pressure group Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) has also pledged support.
The rally comes amid growing criticism of a voter-list revision exercise that has removed 130 million names from the draft rolls across India.
The Election Commission of India (ECI) says the exercise is aimed at updating the voters' list by purging names of people who have died or moved away from their registered addresses.

But opposition parties allege that the exercise - known as the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) - could benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) by removing eligible voters from the rolls.
They accuse the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) and the BJP of "vote chori (theft)".
Both the BJP and the ECI have denied the allegations.

The controversy intensified in September when The Indian Express newspaper in its investigation, external reported that the CEC, Gyanesh Kumar, made key decisions related to the exercise without the agreement of the two other election commissioners, who had raised objections on more than a dozen occasions.
The Election Commission said differences of opinion were normal in any institution and did not affect its functioning.
But concerns over the revision process have continued, with the opposition parties, the CJP and student groups organising a number of protests in Delhi and other Indian cities.

Last month, Congress MP and leader of the opposition Rahul Gandhi led tens of thousands of protesters in a march from Connaught Place in central Delhi to the Supreme Court, seeking the CEC's resignation.

stories.headline: Pahalgam attack chief investigator among recipients of Home Minister’s Medal
stories.title: Pahalgam attack chief investigator among recipients of Home Minister’s Medal
stories.summary: New Delhi, Oct 31: NIA officer Sandeep Chaudhary, who was Chief Investigating Officer in the Pahalgam terror attack case, has been awarded the Union Home Minister's Medal for Excellence in Investigation (Kendriya Grihmantri Dakshata Padak) for 2026. The Ministry of Home Affairs announced the awards on Saturday. Chaudhary has been awarded in the investigation category. He is now posted as Deputy Inspector General in NIA. Chaudhary, a 2012-batch IPS officer of the AGMUT cadre, led the investigation into the April 22, 2025 attack at Baisaran meadow in Pahalgam in which 26 people were killed. NIA took over the case soon after the attack. Hafiz Saeed and Sajid Jatt of Lashkar-e-Toiba were among the accused chargesheeted. Before joining NIA, Chaudhary served as SSP in Shopian, Anantnag, and Srinagar, where he led several counter-insurgency operations. Earlier, Chaudhary's operation led to the arrest of Hizb-ul-Mujahideen commander Syed Naveed Mushtaq alias Naveed Babu along with Deputy Superintendent of Police (DSP) Davinder Singh in 2021. He has received gallantry medals nine times for his role in anti-terror operations in Jammu and Kashmir. He has also received Commendation Discs from the Chief of Army Staff, GOC-in-C Northern Command, the Western Air Command of the IAF, and the Directors General of CRPF, J&K Police, BPR&D, and NIA.

stories.headline: When terror devoured its own
stories.title: When terror devoured its own
stories.summary: The assassinations of Mirwaiz Maulvi Mohammad Farooq on 21 May 1990 and Abdul Ghani Lone on 21 May 2002 expose one of the darkest realities of Pakistan-sponsored terrorism in Jammu and Kashmir. The two killings, occurring exactly twelve years apart, demonstrated that the gun culture promoted in Kashmir was intolerant not merely of those supporting India but even of separatists who questioned the methods and dominance of armed militancy. Neither Mirwaiz Farooq nor Abdul Ghani Lone represented the nationalist political stream. Both questioned Jammu and Kashmir's integration with India and pursued political objectives fundamentally different from India's constitutional position. They were part of the separatist political landscape. Their significance in this historical account arises not from any supposed commitment to Indian nationalism but from their preference for political dialogue over the supremacy of armed terrorism. Their deaths revealed the true character of Pakistan's Kashmir project: political disagreement was acceptable only so long as it remained subordinate to the strategy dictated by Pakistan and its militant proxies. Mirwaiz Farooq Mirwaiz Maulvi Mohammad Farooq occupied an influential religious and political position in Kashmir. His political outlook questioned Jammu and Kashmir's relationship with India, but his approach differed from the increasingly violent militancy that emerged towards the end of the 1980s. He represented an established religious-political institution with an independent following. His influence could not easily be subordinated to newly emerging militant organisations. As Pakistan-sponsored armed militancy expanded its influence, Kashmir's political space began shrinking rapidly. Violence was increasingly used to enforce political conformity. Mirwaiz Farooq was assassinated at his Srinagar residence on 21 May 1990. His killing exposed the vulnerability of independent political leadership in a conflict increasingly controlled by armed organisations. The tragedy was not that India lost a supporter of integration. It was that Kashmir had reached a stage where even those questioning integration could not safely pursue their politics independently of the gun. Abdul Ghani Lone The assassination of Abdul Ghani Lone twelve years later brought this contradiction into even sharper focus. Lone was a prominent separatist and a founding figure of the All Parties Hurriyat Conference. His political position was certainly not aligned with the Indian nationalist perspective. However, Lone increasingly questioned the continuation of armed militancy as the principal instrument for achieving political objectives. He recognised the need for dialogue and political engagement. He was also critical of the influence exercised by foreign militants and external forces over Kashmir's political direction. His approach challenged the strategy of those who wanted the Kashmir conflict to remain permanently dependent upon violence and Pakistani patronage. On 21 May 2002, Lone was assassinated at Eidgah in Srinagar while attending a gathering commemorating the death anniversary of Mirwaiz Farooq. The symbolism could hardly have been more disturbing. A separatist leader attending a memorial for another assassinated separatist became the next victim of the same political culture of violence. His family publicly blamed Pakistan-backed militant elements for his killing. Lone's death exposed a fundamental reality: Pakistan's Kashmir strategy was not necessarily compatible with the political aspirations of Kashmir's own separatist leadership whenever those aspirations departed from its prescribed methods. Pakistan Wanted Control, Not Independent Kashmiri Politics Pakistan has consistently presented its intervention in Jammu and Kashmir as support for the political aspirations of Kashmiris. Yet its sponsorship of armed militancy created conditions in which independent political thinking became increasingly dangerous. The distinction is important. Mirwaiz Farooq and Abdul Ghani Lone were not challenging Pakistan-sponsored militancy because they had accepted India's constitutional position. Their differences concerned political strategy, the role of violence and the possibility of achieving their objectives through dialogue. Even that limited disagreement became unacceptable in an atmosphere dominated by armed extremism. For Pakistan's security establishment, an independently negotiated political settlement carried the danger of diminishing its control over the Kashmir issue. A separatist leader willing to engage in dialogue without submitting to militant dictates could become as inconvenient as a political leader openly supporting India. This was the destructive logic of Pakistan-sponsored terrorism: Kashmir's political future had to remain hostage to the gun, even if the gun ultimately consumed those in whose name the conflict was being conducted. Geelani and the Ideology of Political Rigidity The ideological divisions within separatist politics were equally significant. Syed Ali Shah Geelani represented an uncompromising pro-Pakistan position. His rejection of alternative political formulations and his rigid approach towards dialogue stood in contrast to the more politically flexible positions adopted by leaders such as Lone. Following Lone's assassination, serious allegations emerged from within the separatist establishment itself. A leaked American diplomatic cable subsequently recorded allegations by Lone's sons against Geelani concerning their father's assassination. Mirwaiz Umar Farooq was also reported to have blamed Geelani for his father's killing. These allegations were not judicial findings establishing criminal responsibility. Nevertheless, they demonstrated the depth of suspicion and hostility within the separatist leadership. The ideological question remains unavoidable. When separatist politics itself becomes divided between those favouring dialogue and those insisting upon uncompromising confrontation, the glorification of armed militancy creates an environment in which disagreement can become a matter of life and death. The Admission From Within Hurriyat In January 2011, senior separatist leader Professor Abdul Ghani Bhat made a remarkable public statement concerning political assassinations in Kashmir. He acknowledged that prominent Kashmiri personalities, including Mirwaiz Farooq and Abdul Ghani Lone, had been killed by people from within their own society. His remarks challenged the convenient separatist practice of attributing every prominent political assassination to Indian agencies. The significance of this admission was considerable. It came not from the BJP or any nationalist organisation but from within the separatist political establishment. It exposed the uncomfortable reality that armed militancy had not merely targeted supporters of India. It had also consumed influential personalities belonging to the separatist movement itself. Pakistan's proxy war had created a political environment in which even ideological proximity offered no guarantee of safety. The Larger Tragedy The assassinations of Mirwaiz Farooq and Abdul Ghani Lone must be understood within the broader pattern of terrorism that devastated Jammu and Kashmir. Kashmiri Pandits were subjected to targeted violence, intimidation and displacement. Nationalist political workers were murdered. Ordinary Muslims who refused to cooperate with militant organisations faced threats. Independent political expression increasingly became dangerous. The killings of Mirwaiz Farooq and Lone added another dimension to this pattern. They demonstrated that separatist credentials were themselves insufficient protection. One could question India's integration of Jammu and Kashmir, advocate an alternative political arrangement and still become unacceptable to Pakistan-backed armed extremism merely by questioning its methods. This distinction is essential to an accurate understanding of Kashmir's history. Opposition to terrorism does not automatically establish commitment to Indian nationalism. Equally, separatist politics cannot provide justification for assassination. The two leaders need not be transformed into national heroes to recognise what their killings revealed about the nature of the conflict. The Date That Exposed Pakistan's Contradictions The coincidence of the two assassinations on the same date, twelve years apart, remains one of the most striking chapters of Kashmir's turbulent history. Mirwaiz Farooq was killed on 21 May 1990. Abdul Ghani Lone was killed on 21 May 2002 while attending an event commemorating Farooq's assassination. Both belonged to separatist politics. Both questioned Jammu and Kashmir's relationship with India. Both represented political approaches that did not accept the unquestioned supremacy of armed militancy. Their killings exposed the contradiction between Pakistan's proclaimed support for Kashmiri political aspirations and the violent culture sustained through its proxy organisations. A political movement that cannot tolerate disagreement even within its own ideological constituency cannot credibly claim to be fighting for democratic choice. Conclusion The assassinations of Mirwaiz Farooq and Abdul Ghani Lone should neither be romanticised nor stripped of their political context. They were separatists, not champions of Jammu and Kashmir's integration with India. Their politics remained opposed to the Indian constitutional position. But their preference for dialogue over armed coercion exposed them to the hostility of an extremist political environment that demanded conformity. The allegations surrounding their killings and the subsequent admissions from within the separatist establishment raise enduring questions about the role of Pakistan-backed militancy in eliminating independent political voices. Pakistan's Kashmir project ultimately revealed its own contradiction. It claimed to speak for Kashmiris while nurturing a gun culture that denied Kashmiris the freedom to disagree, including those who broadly shared its opposition to India's position. The assassinations of Mirwaiz and Lone were not the deaths of Indian nationalism's defenders. They were evidence that Pakistan-nurtured terror could devour even its own separatist constituency when it dared to question the supremacy of the gun. That is the dark chapter of Kashmir's history which must neither be forgotten nor politically sanitised. Sunil Sethi, Senior Advocate and Chief Spokesperson, JK BJP

stories.summary: Whenever a society fails its young, someone goes looking for a stranger to blame. In recent weeks, as protests have spread across Europe, that stranger has once again been the Muslim migrant. Foreign political figures, social media influencers and anonymous accounts have attributed the unrest to “invasion,” to Islam’s supposed incompatibility with European values, and to infiltration from abroad. AI-generated images showing France overrun by “hordes of migrants” have circulated widely. The claim is false, and it is also dangerous. It wrongs an entire community, and it diverts attention from the economic and institutional failures that deserve serious scrutiny. Europe is restless again. From Paris to Milan, Madrid to Lisbon, Brussels to Tirana and Athens, students, workers and ordinary citizens have taken to the streets over crumbling public services, unaffordable housing, stagnant wages and rising living costs. Their movements differ in origin and demand. There is no single European uprising with one command or one programme. Taken together, however, they expose a widening gap between what citizens expect of their governments and what those governments are able, or willing, to deliver. Evidence versus propaganda On 21 October, French President Emmanuel Macron rebuked foreign figures for linking Muslim migrants to France’s riots without evidence. He described the circulation of fabricated images as unacceptable and warned of a deliberate manipulation of information by people using France’s turmoil for their own political campaigns. The distinction he drew matters. Those responsible for arson, looting or violence must answer for their acts, but criminal responsibility cannot be assigned to a religious community. Nor do episodes of disorder explain why the demonstrations began. Muslim migrants did not empty French classrooms of teachers. They did not double Lisbon’s rents or erode the purchasing power of households from Rome to Athens. To invoke them is to avoid the harder questions. What the protesters actually want The record is plain. In France, the unrest began with school students protesting overcrowded classrooms, absent teachers and neglected buildings. By mid-October, trade unions and other groups had joined, broadening the demands to wages, pensions and public services. Some gatherings turned violent, and the policing response was harsh; several young protesters have reportedly suffered grave, life-altering injuries. Proportionate policing and the protection of peaceful assembly are not competing goals. A democracy owes its citizens both. In Spain, anger over evictions and soaring rents has become entangled with parliamentary deadlock and an early election. In Portugal, protesters set up housing encampments in Lisbon and Porto; police cleared them on 20 October and arrested dozens. Italy has seen large demonstrations over prices and wages, Belgium over education costs, and Albania over jobs, falling educational standards and allegations of corruption. On 21 October, Greek students and teachers marched over education funding, housing and living costs. One Greek student observed that the government’s rent subsidy did not cover even half his rent. None of these cases is explained by a common religious culprit. Every one of them is explained by the cost of living. The post-war promise The deeper story begins after 1945. Across much of Western Europe, reconstruction and growth underpinned a social settlement that joined private enterprise to public education, healthcare, social insurance and rising household incomes. Its promise was simple. Study and effort would lead to work. Work would support a home and a family. Each generation would enjoy opportunities at least equal to those of its parents. Inequality did not vanish, but social advancement became central to the legitimacy of democratic government. Citizens judged the state not only by its elections and laws but by the security it helped them build. That settlement has been battered repeatedly: by industrial restructuring and globalisation, by the 2008 financial crash and the eurozone debt crisis, by the pandemic, and by successive energy shocks. The damage is cumulative. Families recovering from one setback meet the next before they have rebuilt their savings. Employment can remain high while wages fail to secure a decent life. The OECD’s Employment Outlook 2026 found that real wages in roughly a third of the countries it examined remained below early-2021 levels. In Italy, despite better employment figures, real wages in early 2026 were still well below where they stood five years earlier. Housing: the generational fault line Housing makes the divide visible. According to Eurostat, EU house prices rose 4.7 per cent in the year to the second quarter of 2026; in Portugal the increase was 16.5 per cent. In 2025, young Europeans left their parental homes at an average age of 26.3; in Spain and Italy, the average exceeded 30. Culture plays a part, but so do rents, insecure earnings and a shortage of homes. The owner of a flat bought decades ago watches his wealth grow; a qualified young worker cannot pay the rent. When the value of assets outpaces the rewards of work, faith in merit and mobility begins to crumble. Governments often misread this frustration. They point to falling inflation as proof of recovery, forgetting that prices which surged do not return to old levels. Food, rent, transport and energy still consume household budgets. The war against Iran and the renewed conflict in the Middle East have unsettled energy markets and added to costs, while European governments face rising security expenditure alongside demands for better schools and hospitals. Defence and welfare need not be mutually exclusive, but hard choices require honest public explanation, not slogans and scapegoats. Foreign policy has domestic consequences in another sense too. The Palestinian flag is now a familiar sight at protests across the continent. Many young Europeans feel that their governments have ignored public revulsion at the devastation of Gaza. As the writer Tariq Ali has observed, Vietnam radicalised the generation of 1968; Gaza may be doing the same today. Protest is not the rejection of democracy The comparison with 1968 has limits. Those rebellions arose amid post-war abundance and challenged authority and social convention. Today’s students seek something more immediate: teachers in classrooms, wages that cover expenses, and homes they can afford. Nor should protest be mistaken for a rejection of democracy. The Spring 2026 Eurobarometer recorded substantial satisfaction with democracy at the EU level. Most demonstrators are asking democratic institutions to work better, not to disappear. That is precisely why the scapegoating is so corrosive. When established parties fail to answer real grievances, and when the mainstream lends respectability to anti-migrant narratives, the far right is the beneficiary. Anger that could drive reform is redirected towards a vulnerable minority, and the working class is divided against itself while the causes of its hardship remain untouched. The lesson for India and Kashmir For readers in Jammu and Kashmir, this is not a distant story. Development cannot be measured by inaugurations, investment summits or aggregate growth figures alone. Young people judge it by fair recruitment, functioning colleges, reliable services and a credible route from qualification to employment. We too have seen how easily a convenient minority is offered as an explanation for problems that are, at root, failures of governance. When communal suspicion displaces evidence, legitimate grievances are neglected, trust decays, and the remedies hardship demands are postponed. Europe is neither a single revolutionary camp nor a continent whose institutions have collapsed. But its unrest is a warning about the fraying bond between effort, opportunity and public trust. The post-war compact promised that those who studied, worked and contributed could build secure lives. Many Europeans now doubt that promise will hold for their children. Governments can police violence, debate immigration and contest elections, but none of this will fix unaffordable housing, falling wages or failing services. The storm does not pass because someone else has been blamed for it. It gathers strength when its real causes are left unattended. (The writer is a former Indian Army officer. He writes on issues pertaining to Jammu & Kashmir)

stories.headline: National Conference offers Srinagar-Budgam seat to 3 senior leaders to quell dissent
stories.title: National Conference offers Srinagar-Budgam seat to 3 senior leaders to quell dissent
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 31: The ruling National Conference (NC) has offered the Srinagar-Budgam parliamentary constituency to at least three senior party leaders in an attempt to contain growing dissent following the recent cabinet reshuffle and the impending resignation of incumbent Member of Parliament Aga Syed Ruhullah. According to sources, the party high command has held out the prospect of the parliamentary seat to Jammu and Kashmir Legislative Assembly Speaker Abdul Rahim Rather, six-time legislator Mubarak Gul, and MLA Pampore and former parliamentarian Justice (Retired) Hasnain Masoodi. The move is being seen as part of the party leadership’s efforts to accommodate disgruntled senior leaders and prevent further escalation of internal differences ahead of the likely vacancy in the Srinagar-Budgam Lok Sabha constituency. Confirming that several senior leaders had been approached, Yawar Masoodi, son of MLA Pampore Hasnain Masoodi, told Greater Kashmir that the party leadership was offering the same seat to multiple leaders. “Besides Rather Sahab, they have also offered the seat to (Hasnain) Masoodi Sahab as well as Mubarik Gul Sahab,” he said. The development comes amid uncertainty over the party’s organisational arrangements and mounting discontent among sections of its legislators following the expansion of Chief Minister Omar Abdullah’s Council of Ministers on October 27. Six-time MLA from Eidgah Mubarak Gul, who was appointed NC General Secretary after the cabinet reshuffle but just three days later removed, said he would disclose details about developments within the party at a press conference scheduled for November 4. Speaking to Greater Kashmir , Gul said he was currently trying to pacify his supporters, who had been organising protests over his exclusion from the government. “Right now I am pacifying my workers as they have been organising Kafan rallies and Mashaal rallies in the constituency,” he said. The reported offer of the Srinagar-Budgam parliamentary seat to multiple senior leaders comes a day after Greater Kashmir reported the party leadership’s consideration of Rather as a possible candidate for the constituency. Rather, a seven-time legislator from Charar-e-Sharief in central Kashmir’s Budgam district, currently serves as Speaker of the Jammu and Kashmir Legislative Assembly. He was elected to the post in November 2024. Any decision to field Rather for the parliamentary constituency would require him to relinquish his current position of Speaker Legislative Assembly. However, according to sources, Rather has informed the NC high command that it should instead field his daughter, Dr Shagufta Rather from the Srinagar-Budgam constituency. The party is also reportedly considering senior MLA Gurez Nazir Ahmad Khan (Gurezi) for the Assembly Speaker’s post, although Khan told Greater Kashmir that he had not been informed about any such proposal. The developments are unfolding against the backdrop of the announced resignation of Aga Syed Ruhullah from both the NC and his Lok Sabha membership on November 3. Ruhullah’s office has confirmed that the Srinagar MP intends to resign from the party and Parliament on that date, citing differences with the party leadership over electoral commitments, including restoration of Article 370, protection of constitutional rights and the release of prisoners. His departure would create a vacancy in the Srinagar-Budgam parliamentary constituency, setting the stage for a possible by-election. The parliamentary seat has consequently emerged as a potential point of discussion within the party as its leadership faces pressure from several senior legislators who were left out of the recent cabinet expansion. On October 27, four legislators were inducted into Chief Minister Omar Abdullah’s Council of Ministers. However, more than a dozen NC MLAs were conspicuous by their absence from the swearing-in ceremony, with reports attributing their absence to dissatisfaction over ministerial appointments and regional representation. Senior NC leaders subsequently reached out to some of the disgruntled legislators, including Gurezi, amid reports of resentment over their exclusion from the expanded cabinet. On Friday, a group of 17 NC legislators and independent MLA from Thanamandi also held a meeting at the Srinagar residence of MLA Lolab Qaiser Jamsheed Lone to discuss developments within the party. Separately, 18 NC legislators on Saturday submitted a memorandum to CM Omar seeking a series of corrective measures, including cabinet restructuring, ministerial accountability, changes in the Chief Minister’s advisory mechanism, greater consultation with elected representatives, and organisational reforms. The legislators also sought the constitution of a high-level committee to monitor implementation of the party’s election manifesto and called for renewed political mobilisation for restoration of J&K’s statehood and protection of its constitutional identity. The reported distribution of the Srinagar-Budgam parliamentary seat among several prospective candidates adds another dimension to the party’s efforts to manage internal differences. While Rather’s name had earlier emerged as a possible choice for the constituency, the reported approaches to Gul and Masoodi suggest that the party leadership is also considering other senior leaders for the seat.

stories.headline: 6 Indian tourists go missing during trek to deepest lake of Nepal, Shey-Phoksundo
stories.title: 6 Indian tourists go missing during trek to deepest lake of Nepal, Shey-Phoksundo
stories.summary: Kathmandu , November 1 : Six Indian tourists have gone missing during a trek to Shey-Phoksundo Lake, the deepest lake of Nepal, after heavy snowfall in the area, officials confirmed. The India tourists, who include two women and four men, are confirmed to have gone missing while travelling from Ward Nos. 4 and 8 of Dolpo Buddha Rural Municipality towards Shey-Phoksundo Lake. They were last reported missing in the Numla Pass and Bagla Pass areas between Ward Nos. 4 and 8 of Shey-Phoksundo Rural Municipality. Local guides suspect that the tourists may have become stranded following heavy snowfall in the Himalayan region, reportedly influenced by Cyclone Arnab developing in the Bay of Bengal. According to local officials, the tourists proceeded towards the high-altitude area despite warnings from residents that crossing the mountain passes would be difficult due to snowfall. They are believed to have become trapped in the snow while returning. Dolpa Chief District Officer Junu Hamal confirmed that “the tourists became stranded while returning from Dho towards Phoksundo Lake.” She said, “They had been warned by locals about the difficult weather and mountain conditions but proceeded with their journey.” Shey-Phoksundo Rural Municipality Chairman Dhawa Samduk Gurung said, “Mobile phone communication is unavailable in the mountain passes between Wards 4 and 8, making it difficult to obtain information about the tourists’ whereabouts and current condition.” According to the District Administration Office, “A total of 244 tourists have reached Upper Dolpa. Of them, 149 are Nepali nationals, 44 are from SAARC countries, and 51 are citizens of other foreign countries.” In view of the adverse weather conditions, the district administration has urged tourists to avoid risky areas and remain in safe locations. Tourist arrivals in the Shey-Phoksundo Lake area have been increasing in recent years. According to available data, 4,882 tourists visited Phoksundo Lake during the first 11 months of the fiscal year 2082/83. Dolpa Deputy Superintendent of Police Anil Raj Giri said, “Six Indian tourists remain out of contact, according to the latest information.” Further adding, “Authorities have requested the concerned agency to arrange a helicopter for search and rescue operations.” Search and rescue efforts have been hampered by heavy snowfall and adverse weather conditions in the high Himalayan region. The absence of mobile phone connectivity in the area and thick snow have made it difficult to determine the tourists’ whereabouts and condition. A team of the Nepal Army has also been deployed to locate the tourists and assist in their rescue. (ANI)

stories.headline: Cybercrime, drugs among J&K’s biggest challenges: IGP Kashmir
stories.title: Cybercrime, drugs among J&K’s biggest challenges: IGP Kashmir
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 31: Inspector General of Police (IGP) Kashmir Sujit Kumar on Saturday identified cybercrime and the growing drug menace among the biggest challenges confronting Jammu and Kashmir, asserting that the police were prepared to tackle emerging threats while safeguarding national unity and security. Speaking to reporters at the historic Ghanta Ghar in Lal Chowk on the sidelines of Rashtriya Ekta Diwas celebrations, the IGP said the nature of challenges facing law enforcement agencies was evolving, with cybercrime and narcotics emerging as major areas of concern. “Cybercrime is one of the biggest challenges, both today and in the coming days. Along with the drug menace, there are other activities directed against our country, and Jammu and Kashmir is looking at these challenges from a new perspective,” Kumar said. He said the police would elaborate separately on the measures being undertaken to address these concerns, stressing that the occasion was dedicated to celebrating national unity and integrity. The Kashmir Police chief’s remarks came as security forces, police personnel, students and young people gathered at Lal Chowk to participate in National Unity Day celebrations marking the birth anniversary of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel. Describing Lal Chowk as a historic witness to the celebrations, Kumar said the gathering had provided an opportunity for people in Kashmir to join the nationwide observance of Rashtriya Ekta Diwas. “Today, we celebrated Ekta Diwas at historic Lal Chowk. We witnessed the live broadcast of the Ekta Diwas parade from Kevadia in Gujarat, where the Prime Minister addressed the nation,” he said. The IGP said Lieutenant Governor Manoj Sinha, personnel from Jammu and Kashmir Police and Central Armed Police Forces, schoolchildren and Kashmiri youth participated in the programme and listened to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's address. Referring to the Prime Minister's message, Kumar said the occasion had reinforced the responsibility of citizens and security agencies to protect the country's unity and integrity. “The Prime Minister has given us the responsibility of safeguarding the unity and integrity of the country. Whatever challenges come before the police and security forces in the coming days, we are prepared to face them,” he said. Asked specifically about the growing threat of cybercrime and the steps being taken to counter it, the IGP acknowledged the seriousness of the challenge but said a detailed discussion on the issue would be held separately. He also referred to the narcotics problem and activities threatening national security, indicating that the police were approaching these challenges with renewed focus. Kumar, however, emphasised that the immediate significance of the day lay in celebrating the country's unity and collective commitment to national integrity. “Today is the day of national unity, the day of the country's togetherness. We should celebrate it. I extend my greetings to everyone on National Unity Day,” he said.

opening: Srinagar, Oct 31: Inspector General of Police (IGP) Kashmir Sujit Kumar on Saturday identified cybercrime and the growing drug menace among the biggest challenges confronting Jammu and Kashmir, asserting that the police were prepared to tackle emerging threats while safeguarding national unity and security.

Speaking to reporters at the historic Ghanta Ghar in Lal Chowk on the sidelines of Rashtriya Ekta Diwas celebrations, the IGP said the nature of challenges facing law enforcement agencies was evolving, with cybercrime and narcotics emerging as major areas of concern.
body: “Cybercrime is one of the biggest challenges, both today and in the coming days.
Along with the drug menace, there are other activities directed against our country, and Jammu and Kashmir is looking at these challenges from a new perspective,” Kumar said.
He said the police would elaborate separately on the measures being undertaken to address these concerns, stressing that the occasion was dedicated to celebrating national unity and integrity.
The Kashmir.

Police chief’s remarks came as security forces, police personnel, students and young people gathered at Lal Chowk to participate in National Unity Day celebrations marking the birth anniversary of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel.
Describing Lal Chowk as a historic witness to the celebrations, Kumar said the gathering had provided an opportunity for people in Kashmir to join the nationwide observance of Rashtriya Ekta Diwas.
“Today, we celebrated Ekta Diwas at historic Lal Chowk.
We witnessed the live broadcast of the Ekta Diwas parade from Kevadia in Gujarat, where the Prime Minister addressed the nation,” he said.
The IGP said Lieutenant Governor Manoj Sinha, personnel from Jammu and Kashmir.
Police and Central Armed Police Forces, schoolchildren and Kashmiri youth participated in the programme and listened to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's address.
Referring to the Prime Minister's message, Kumar said the occasion had reinforced the responsibility of citizens and security agencies to protect the country's unity and integrity.
“The Prime Minister has given us the responsibility of safeguarding the unity and integrity of the country.
Whatever challenges come before the police and security forces in the coming days, we are prepared to face them,” he said.

Asked specifically about the growing threat of cybercrime and the steps being taken to counter it, the IGP acknowledged the seriousness of the challenge but said a detailed discussion on the issue would be held separately.
He also referred to the narcotics problem and activities threatening national security, indicating that the police were approaching these challenges with renewed focus.
Kumar, however, emphasised that the immediate significance of the day lay in celebrating the country's unity and collective commitment to national integrity.
“Today is the day of national unity, the day of the country's togetherness.
We should celebrate it.
I extend my greetings to everyone on National Unity Day,” he said.

stories.title: From Land to the Tiller to the Loss of Political Voice
stories.summary: There are moments in the life of a society when the present becomes so overwhelming that it begins to obscure the lessons of its own past. Political uncertainty, administrative helplessness and collective disillusionment can leave a people questioning not merely where they are headed, but whether they have lost sight of what they once stood for. At such moments, history is more than a record of yesterday. It becomes a compass for tomorrow. Jammu and Kashmir finds itself at precisely such a juncture. The prevailing political atmosphere is marked by an unsettling contradiction. Administratively, the elected dispensation appears constrained, frequently unable or unwilling to assert even the limited authority available to it. Politically, however, where it could still exercise its voice, articulate dissent and hold the Union Government accountable, it has too often retreated into a silence that increasingly resembles political surrender. This is accompanied by a tacit willingness to dilute its political position, lower the pitch of its dissent and project an image of weakness and helplessness. One is compelled to ask: what has this political accommodation achieved? Has it brought relief to young people languishing in distant jails? Has it secured greater dignity, employment or institutional safeguards for the people? Has it advanced the restoration of statehood or strengthened the democratic character of governance? If compromise is to be defended as political pragmatism, it must produce something tangible. Otherwise, it risks becoming an end in itself, leaving the public with neither political assertion nor administrative dividends. To appreciate the depth of this moment, it is worth revisiting the political journey that shaped modern Jammu and Kashmir. When the Jammu and Kashmir Constituent Assembly convened in 1951, it was not merely another legislative institution. It was entrusted with the formidable task of defining the political, constitutional and socio-economic future of a society emerging from feudal structures and historical inequalities. Its debates were about far more than the mechanics of governance. They concerned the dignity of the individual, the redistribution of opportunity, access to education and the relationship between political power and public welfare. The Assembly brought together individuals of remarkable intellectual and political distinction, among them Sheikh Mohammad Abdullah, Mirza Mohammad Afzal Beg, D.P. Dhar, Girdhari Lal Dogra and Ghulam Ahmad Mir of Sallar, my grandfather. They belonged to a generation that, whatever their differences, understood politics as an instrument of social transformation. Their politics was rooted in the conviction that public authority carried an obligation to improve the lives of ordinary citizens. My grandfather occupied a particularly interesting place in that generation. Educated at Punjab University, Lahore, Ghulam Ahmad Mir combined intellectual refinement with an intimate understanding of rural society. His academic grounding enabled him to engage with legislative questions and agrarian economics, but his sensibilities remained firmly rooted in the villages of Dachinpara and the Lidder Valley. His social position made his political choices even more consequential. He was himself a Zaildar of Sallar, an institution historically associated with exploitation, feudal privilege, authority and extraction. Yet his legacy, as remembered by generations in the area, was markedly different. He belonged to a different mould. Rather than treating influence as an instrument of personal enrichment, he sought to employ it for education, social uplift and community welfare. He was remembered not simply as a man of standing, but as someone who believed that privilege carried responsibilities. His civic and spiritual convictions were reflected in institutions that continue to form part of Pahalgam's collective memory. The historic Jamia Masjid of Pahalgam, whose foundation was laid in 1932, stands in striking alignment with the local Gurdwara and Temple. This shared spatial arrangement has endured as a visible expression of the area's tradition of communal coexistence, rather than being merely an architectural coincidence. His contributions to the expansion and service, or Khidmah, of the sacred Khiram Dargah Hazratbal were another manifestation of his spiritual commitment. He left his home and spent five long years staying there. But his vision extended beyond religious and civic institutions. It reached the fields, the orchards and, above all, the minds of the people. Dachinpara and its adjoining areas were traditionally dependent on dry almond cultivation, an agricultural model increasingly vulnerable to climatic and geographical limitations. With considerable foresight, he encouraged the introduction of apple cultivation, helping initiate an agricultural transition that would eventually reshape the economic landscape of the region. His interest in the environment was equally evident in his afforestation efforts across otherwise barren mountain slopes. His home, Darul Khair in Sallar, too, became a centre of social interaction, intellectual exchange and hospitality. Long before Pahalgam evolved into the commercial tourist destination it is today, travellers, scholars and ordinary people from different walks of life found a welcome there. It was an expression of hospitality that was not measured by commercial returns, but by the dignity extended to a guest. Yet perhaps the most consequential expression of his convictions was his engagement with the politics of land, education and social emancipation. The historical proceedings of the Constituent Assembly offer an important window into this aspect of his public life. As a Zaildar with substantial landed interests, he had every conventional incentive to defend the privileges of his class when the Assembly debated radical agrarian reforms. Instead, he supported the principle of Land to the Tiller and the abolition of large landed estates. The significance of this position cannot be understood without recalling the conditions of the Kashmiri peasantry. For generations, cultivators had worked land they did not own, with the fruits of their labour disproportionately accruing to landlords. The agrarian reforms represented a fundamental challenge to this inherited inequality. Alongside Sheikh Abdullah and other proponents of the reforms, my grandfather supported the transfer of ownership to the actual tiller, without imposing an oppressive compensation burden that could have defeated the very purpose of emancipation. In doing so, he was willing to see his own landed interests subordinated to a larger social transformation. His understanding of emancipation, however, did not end with land redistribution. He recognised that ownership could liberate the peasant economically, but education was essential to liberate the next generation intellectually. He therefore invested personal resources in the education of young people from Dachinpara, facilitating opportunities for promising students to pursue studies outside the region, including at institutions such as Khalsa College, Amritsar. The educational vision reflected in the Assembly's early constitutional framework was equally remarkable. The commitment to free education demonstrated an understanding that social equality could not be achieved through economic redistribution alone. Long before the Indian Constitution's 86th Amendment formally inserted Article 21A, the foundational constitutional thinking in Jammu and Kashmir had recognised education as central to the state's obligations. This was the political imagination of that generation: land for the tiller, education for the child, dignity for the individual and responsibility for those entrusted with public authority. Seven decades later, the landscape has changed dramatically. The events of August 5, 2019, the abrogation of Articles 370 and 35A, and the subsequent reorganisation of the erstwhile state into two Union Territories fundamentally altered Jammu and Kashmir's constitutional and political arrangement. The loss of statehood and the transfer of significant governing powers to the Union have left elected institutions functioning within a considerably diminished framework. The Supreme Court's judgment may have brought the constitutional litigation to a conclusion, and its authority as the guardian of the Constitution commands respect. But a judicial conclusion does not necessarily settle the political anxieties of an entire society. A people's attachment to their identity, democratic agency and political aspirations cannot simply be extinguished by the closure of a courtroom proceeding. The subsequent Assembly elections witnessed substantial public participation. That participation was not necessarily an endorsement of the prevailing constitutional arrangement or an expression of complete satisfaction with the political choices available. For many, it was an assertion of democratic agency, an attempt to reclaim political space and a rejection of the idea that Jammu and Kashmir could be governed indefinitely without an elected government accountable to its people. Yet, following the elections, an uncomfortable political quietude has settled over much of the public discourse. The conversation has increasingly narrowed to potholes, erratic electricity schedules, dry taps, dysfunctional schools and the familiar catalogue of administrative grievances. These issues are undeniably important. They affect everyday life and demand urgent attention. But they cannot become the entire vocabulary of politics in a place whose constitutional and political circumstances remain so profoundly unsettled. The elected leadership appears caught between two competing realities: the responsibility to administer an institutionally weakened Union Territory and the obligation to articulate the larger political aspirations that brought it to power. This raises a fundamental question: is Jammu and Kashmir suffering from political disenfranchisement, administrative failure, or both? The uncomfortable answer is that these conditions reinforce one another. When meaningful legislative and executive authority is diminished, accountability becomes fragmented. Decisions travel through layers of bureaucracy, responsibilities become blurred and elected representatives find themselves explaining outcomes over which they may exercise limited control. Governance risks becoming an exercise in managing files rather than resolving people's problems. At the same time, when citizens are compelled to devote their energies to basic necessities, their capacity to engage with larger questions of constitutional rights, democratic representation and political accountability inevitably suffers. The daily struggle for electricity, water, employment and functioning public institutions gradually displaces the more fundamental debate about the structure of power itself. This is perhaps the most dangerous consequence of the present arrangement: the gradual normalisation of diminished political expectations. But the responsibility for this situation cannot be placed entirely at the door of constitutional circumstances. Political leadership must also be judged by how it responds to constraints. An elected government cannot use its limited mandate as a permanent explanation for its silences, just as it cannot invoke constitutional grievances to excuse failures in everyday administration. Political assertion and administrative competence are not competing responsibilities. They are complementary obligations. It is here that the contrast with the generation of 1951 becomes particularly instructive. Those leaders did not ask the peasant to choose between the title deed to his land and his political voice. They understood that the two were inseparable. They challenged feudal privilege while constructing institutions of governance. They pursued agrarian reform while expanding educational opportunities. They understood that political dignity without economic empowerment was incomplete, just as material progress without democratic agency could never constitute genuine emancipation. Today, unfortunately, much of our political discourse has descended into transactional calculations, personality contests and relentless character assassination. Public life is increasingly consumed by arguments over individuals rather than ideas, positions rather than principles and political survival rather than public purpose. The people of Jammu and Kashmir deserve better. They deserve a leadership capable of articulating their constitutional aspirations without ambiguity, defending their democratic rights without hesitation and delivering administrative results without excuses. They deserve political representatives who understand that dissent is not disloyalty, that accommodation is not an achievement in itself and that holding public office is a responsibility rather than a privilege. Remembering Mir-e-Sallar and his contemporaries is not an exercise in nostalgia, nor is it an attempt to romanticise an earlier political era. Their generation had its own contradictions, limitations and difficult choices. But it left behind an important standard by which public life can still be judged: the willingness to place collective interest above personal advantage. For me, this inheritance is both personal and political. The history of my grandfather is not merely a family memory. It is a reminder of what public responsibility once demanded from those who occupied position of influence. A man who could have defended his interests chose to support their redistribution. A man of social standing invested in the education of those who had little access to opportunity. A man rooted in his own community understood the importance of coexistence beyond it. That is the kind of political courage our times urgently require. The most meaningful tribute to the founding generation would not be to celebrate their photographs, repeat their speeches or invoke their names at public gatherings. It would be to recover the principles that informed their public lives: integrity, intellectual courage, social responsibility and an unwavering commitment to the dignity of ordinary people. History does not offer a ready-made solution to the crises of the present. But it does remind us that political limitations need not become limitations of political imagination. Jammu and Kashmir must not surrender to the belief that administrative survival requires political silence, or that constitutional aspirations can be postponed indefinitely in the name of pragmatic governance. Neither should political rhetoric become an alibi for administrative incompetence. A society cannot live indefinitely on memories, but it can draw strength from them. The covenant of 1951 was, at its heart, a promise that power must serve the people, that dignity must accompany development and that political institutions must remain answerable to those in whose name they function. Perhaps the most urgent task before our present generation is not to invent a new political vocabulary, but to rediscover the courage to honour that old promise. For a people who once fought to reclaim their land, their education and their dignity, the greatest tragedy would be to become reconciled to the loss of their political voice. The author is an Advocate and Columnist on Politics and Governance.
